explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The writer says, “As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul longs after You, O God.” He isn't longing for something God hands out. He's longing for God. Think of me lunging at the cooling rack the second the timer dings, except his lunge is aimed at the best possible target.

Easy mistake, friend, since the verse is full of water. But the streams are the picture, and the deer is the comparison. What the writer's soul longs after is “You, O God” (Psalm 42:1). Rain never shows up in this psalm.

Close, but this psalm never mentions a long life. Right after the deer, the writer says his soul thirsts “for God, the living God” (Psalm 42:2). If anything, his days already feel long, since his tears go on both day and night (Psalm 42:3). The longing is for God, not for more days.

Listen to the question again: “When shall I come and appear in God’s presence?” You don't ask WHEN you'll arrive if you're already standing in the doorway. The writer is thirsting for the living God, and I think that's a man who hasn't gotten there yet. Longing is the whole mood of this verse.

Right, it's False. The writer asks, “When shall I come and appear in God’s presence?” (Psalm 42:2). That's a man looking ahead to a day, not a man standing in the room. I think he's still on his way, and he's thirsty the whole walk.

Yes, friend. While he cries, men ask him all day long, “Where is your God?” (Psalm 42:3). It comes back later, when his enemies taunt him “all day long” with the very same question (Psalm 42:10). Same question, twice, and it never takes a day off.

Nice try, because the psalm does have a “why” question. But the writer asks that one to himself: “Why are you downcast, O my soul?” (Psalm 42:5). The people around him ask something else, and it's about God: “Where is your God?” (Psalm 42:3).

That question isn't in these verses. The text says men ask him “all day long” where his God is (Psalm 42:3). It doesn't say they accuse him of anything. Stick to what the verse says, and the answer is sitting right there.

explanations.answer: Full of shouts of joy and praise
explanations.explanation: That's the one. He remembers leading the festive procession to the house of God “with shouts of joy and praise” (Psalm 42:4). Shouts, baker! That's a crowd with its whole voice turned on. I think remembering a day like that hits hard when your tears are your food now.

Not this walk. The writer remembers it with “shouts of joy and praise” (Psalm 42:4). The worry and unease show up in the present, when he asks his soul why it's downcast (Psalm 42:5). The memory itself is loud and happy.

The weeping belongs to now, not to that walk. Right before this, he says his tears have been his food day and night (Psalm 42:3). What he remembers is leading a festive procession “with shouts of joy and praise” (Psalm 42:4). That's a pretty big gap between then and now.

Yes, hope. He tells his soul, “Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him for the salvation of His presence” (Psalm 42:5). Notice he doesn't say the soul feels better yet. He says to aim it at God and keep going. That's a solid talking-to.

Fear is a fair guess, since the writer is clearly hurting. But the verse says something different: “Put your hope in God” (Psalm 42:5). His soul already has plenty of unease. The instruction is to hand it something better to hold.
I get why you'd pick it with a soul this downcast. But the psalm never says shame. It says, “Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him” (Psalm 42:5). Hope is what he gives his soul to hold.

That's right. The writer says, “my soul despairs within me. Therefore I remember You from the land of Jordan and the peaks of Hermon” (Psalm 42:6). Look at that word “Therefore.” The despair is the very reason he starts remembering God. He reaches for Him instead of letting go.

It sounds like it would fit, with his soul in despair. But look at what he actually says: “Therefore I remember You…” (Psalm 42:6). He admits the despair out loud, and then he turns toward God. No doubting in that line.

No leaving here, friend. He says, “O my God, my soul despairs within me. Therefore I remember You from the land of Jordan…” (Psalm 42:6). He calls Him “my God” in the same breath. He's holding on, not walking out.

True. He says, “Deep calls to deep in the roar of Your waterfalls; all Your breakers and waves have rolled over me” (Psalm 42:7). Your waterfalls, Your breakers, Your waves. He's saying that he's under water, and he's telling God whose water it is.

The writer actually says it's God's: “all Your breakers and waves have rolled over me” (Psalm 42:7). The waterfalls are called “Your waterfalls” in the same verse. He's talking to God while the waves roll over him. That's a bold way to pray.

That's it. The verse says, “The LORD decrees His loving devotion by day, and at night His song is with me as a prayer to the God of my life” (Psalm 42:8). Day has devotion, night has a song. Even in the dark, he isn't left without something with him.
I can see why you'd guess it, given the mood so far. But the verse says, “at night His song is with me as a prayer to the God of my life” (Psalm 42:8). A song, not silence. Night is when it shows up.
That's a cozy guess, baker, but dreams don't appear in this verse. What's with him at night is “His song,” and it's “a prayer to the God of my life” (Psalm 42:8). Nobody's sleeping through it.

Yes. He says to God, “Why have You forgotten me?” (Psalm 42:9). That's the writer's honest question, said straight to God, whom he's just called “my Rock.” I think it takes real trust to bring a question that hard right to Him.
Not this time. The writer asks, “Why have You forgotten me?” (Psalm 42:9). Chosen would be a happy question, and he's asking a hurting one. He's walking in sorrow, and he says so.

Tested doesn't show up here. He says to God his Rock, “Why have You forgotten me?” (Psalm 42:9). Then he asks why he must walk in sorrow because of the enemy’s oppression. It's a question, plain and raw.

That's the one. He says, “Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him, my Savior and my God” (Psalm 42:11). The first time he told his soul to hope, he didn't add that. This time he calls God his Savior. It's a good line to hold on to.
Those words aren't in this verse. He does mention a song at night in Psalm 42:8, but that's the LORD's song. In Psalm 42:11 he calls God “my Savior and my God.”
That pairing doesn't appear here. Earlier he called God “my Rock” (Psalm 42:9). In this verse he says, “I will yet praise Him, my Savior and my God” (Psalm 42:11).

Right. He prays, “deliver me from deceitful and unjust men” (Psalm 43:1). Right alongside it, he asks God to plead his case against an ungodly nation. He's naming exactly what he needs help with, and I say that's a good way to pray.

That sounds like something you'd hear in a psalm, but not this one. The writer asks to be delivered “from deceitful and unjust men” (Psalm 43:1). He doesn't mention rulers here. Stick with what the verse says.
No friends show up in this prayer. He asks God to deliver him “from deceitful and unjust men” (Psalm 43:1). The words are deceitful and unjust, which is a lot heavier than idle.
Yes, baker. He says, “For You are the God of my refuge. Why have You rejected me?” (Psalm 43:2). He says who God is to him, and then he asks the hard question anyway. Both are in the same breath.
That phrase isn't in this verse. Right before he asks his question, he says, “For You are the God of my refuge” (Psalm 43:2). A refuge is a place you run to for safety.
Not here, friend. The verse says, “For You are the God of my refuge” (Psalm 43:2). It's personal: my refuge. He's talking about what God is to him.

explanations.answer: Lead him to where God dwells
explanations.explanation: Yes. He prays, “Send out Your light and Your truth; let them lead me. Let them bring me to Your holy mountain and to the place where You dwell” (Psalm 43:3). Light and truth are the guides, and God's dwelling place is the destination. Sounds like the best set of directions you could ask for.

The writer isn't asking for that. He says of God's light and truth, “let them lead me” (Psalm 43:3). He wants to be brought to God's holy mountain and the place where He dwells. The light is for his path.
That's not in this verse. He asks that God's light and truth “lead me” and “bring me to Your holy mountain and to the place where You dwell” (Psalm 43:3). The request is about being led to God.
That's it. He says he will go “to the altar of God, to God, my greatest joy” (Psalm 43:4). Not just a joy, but his GREATEST joy. When a man with tears for food says that, I believe him.
It makes sense that you'd think so, with how heavy this psalm gets. But the writer says, “to God, my greatest joy” (Psalm 43:4). Joy is the word he lands on.
He does ask hard questions in this psalm. Still, what he says is, “to God, my greatest joy” (Psalm 43:4). It's joy, and he says it right at the altar.

The text says the opposite. He says, “Then I will go to the altar of God, to God, my greatest joy. I will praise You with the harp, O God, my God” (Psalm 43:4). Nobody's zipping their lips at that altar. He's bringing a harp.
Right, it's False. He says, “I will praise You with the harp, O God, my God” (Psalm 43:4). That's praise with sound, strings and all. I think he's planning something good.
Yes, the harp. He says, “I will praise You with the harp, O God, my God” (Psalm 43:4). He's got the instrument picked out already. That's a man who is planning on praising.
A trumpet would be loud, but that's not what he says. The verse says, “I will praise You with the harp, O God, my God” (Psalm 43:4). Strings, not brass.
Good instrument, wrong psalm. He says he'll praise God “with the harp” (Psalm 43:4). No tambourine in these verses.
